General information.Name: Life cycle assessment of nine representative agroindustrial systems of sugar production in Mexico
General information.Category: Manufacturing/311 Food Manufacturing/3113 Sugar and Confectionery Product Manufacturing
General information.Description: Mexico is the sixth-largest producer of sucrose worldwide. Therefore, evaluating the environmental impacts of Mexican sugar and proposing impact mitigation strategies is of high importance since this would support better environmental performance and foster competition within the sector. However, the technological variability that occurs between farms and sugar mills, together with the different types of sugar that are produced, makes it difficult to identify a single agro-industrial production system for sugar production, that represents the entire sector. Environmental improvement strategies identified for one system are specific and have a low level of applicability to others. Therefore, the aim of this study is to develop a life cycle assessment study of nine representative sugar production systems in Mexico, considering 1 ton of sugar as a functional unit while also considering the types of sugar and technological level. The nine sugar life cycle systems analyzed were classified as follows: standard conventional (SC), standard semimechanized (SSM), standard mechanized (SM), refined conventional (RC), refined semimechanized (RSM), refined mechanized (RM), muscovado conventional (MC), muscovado semimechanized (MSM) and muscovado mechanized (MM). The results showed that conventional systems demonstrated a better environmental performance for all the impact categories analyzed, primarily because they have a lower energy requirement in cultivation and irrigation, require less fertilizers and applied pesticides, and in the industrial stage, require less chemicals for clarification. Regarding the types of sugar, Muscovado presented the lowest environmental impacts in all the categories analyzed, since it only requires one crystallization and centrifugation process, followed by drying, which is associated with lower requirements for electricity, heat, and steams. The results would suggest that the strategic avenues for further improving the environmental profile of sugarcane production and processing could include (a) continued pursuit of high yields, which is an important determinant of the environmental impacts of agricultural products, (b) precision application of fertilizers to reduce the potential for losses to the environment and (c) maximizing the utilization of coproducts to increase environmental credits.
General information.Tags: Life cycle assessment of sugar, Environmental impacts of sugar, Mexican sugar, Sugarcane, Standard sugar, Muscovado sugar, Refined sugar, LCA of sugar
General information.Technology Description: The life cycle assessment was conducted using SimaPro 8.1.1.16 software and the ReCiPe midpoint (H) V1.12 method for impact assessment. System classification was based on hierarchical cluster analysis performed with IBM SPSS Statistics 20. The life cycle inventory was constructed using primary data and supplemented with data from the Ecoinvent database V3 for missing background processes.

processDocumentation.LCI method: Process-based attributional LCA. The study follows a life cycle perspective from agricultural production to distribution of sugar and co-products.
processDocumentation.Modeling constants: Capital goods such as tractors and harvesters were excluded from the system boundary. Cogeneration was not considered due to its limited use in the studied context. For the conventional system, 89.25% of the sugarcane harvested area is subjected to burning. Biomass generation is assumed to be 18.2 tons per hectare. Nitrogen loss from soil by burning is assumed to be 11 kg per hectare.
processDocumentation.Data source information: Primary data was gathered from consultations with technicians of national and local associations of sugar cane producers, interviews with officials of the National Committee for Sustainable Development of Sugar Cane (CONADESUCA), and surveys conducted with Sugar Cane Producers. Secondary data was sourced from sugarcane production statistics for the 2016/2017 harvest (CONADESUCA-SAGARPA, 2017) and the Ecoinvent V3 database.
processDocumentation.Data completeness: The study covers the main stages of sugar production: agricultural production, sugar milling, commercialization, and the production of coproducts (ethanol and fodder). It is representative of the State of Veracruz, which accounts for 42% of the cultivated area and 37.10% of sucrose production in Mexico.
processDocumentation.Data selection: The study is based on data from 18 sugar mills in Veracruz, Mexico. Nine representative systems were defined based on technological level (conventional, semi-mechanized, mechanized) and sugar type (standard, refined, muscovado). This extraction focuses on the 'standard conventional' scenario. Capital goods were excluded from the analysis due to their long lifespan.
processDocumentation.Data treatment: Hierarchical cluster analysis was used to classify the technological levels of the 18 sugar mills. Average data for the resulting clusters were used to build the LCI for the representative scenarios.
processDocumentation.Sampling procedure: Data was collected through a combination of expert consultations, surveys with producers, interviews with government officials, and a review of official statistics and relevant literature.
processDocumentation.Use advice: The environmental improvement strategies identified are specific to the systems analyzed and may have low applicability to other contexts. The results are specific to the conditions of the sugarcane industry in Veracruz, Mexico. The system boundary excludes the manufacturing and end-of-life of capital equipment and does not consider cogeneration.
processDocumentation.Completeness: The study is comprehensive within its defined scope (cradle-to-distribution), covering all major process stages and co-products. However, it explicitly excludes capital equipment, which represents a completeness gap.
